### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

For a 13-page Educational Researcher feature, the paper assembles a competent and genuinely interdisciplinary citation base — adult education program evaluation, the political-economy literature on deservingness and redistribution, state appropriations determinants, and cost-disease theory — and is unusually candid that it is not a comprehensive account. But its coverage is one-directional on the two questions that carry the argument: it cites work showing immigration depresses public goods spending without engaging the substantial conflicting evidence, and it omits the immigration-enforcement 'chilling effects' literature entirely, even though that is the leading demand-side rival to its supply-side conclusion. Readers can trust the paper's descriptive record and its characterization of the adult education evaluation literature; they should treat its causal framing as resting on a narrower and more contested evidence base than the text implies.

**Strengths:**

- Genuinely cross-disciplinary for an education venue: economics of education (Mincer 1974; Hanushek et al. 2015; Baumol 1993; Archibald & Feldman 2008), political science and political economy (Wlezien 1995; Soroka & Wlezien 2005; Gilens 2009; Poterba 1994; Weingast et al. 1981), sociology (Lanford & Quadagno 2022; Van Oorschot 2006), and higher education finance (Delaney & Doyle 2011; Okunade 2004) are all put to work rather than name-checked.
- The adult education evidence base is characterized accurately and with appropriate hedging. The claim that causal research on returns is 'limited' is correctly attributed to Kim & Belzer (2021), and the welfare-to-work experimental evidence (Hamilton et al. 2001; Hotz et al. 2006) and the nonexperimental LSAL work (Reder 2019) are described with the right epistemic weight — 'associated with' for Reder, not 'caused.'
- The paper is honest about the limits of its own conceptual model, explicitly flagging unmeasured demand-side factors (private learning tools, micro-credentials) it cannot rule out — a rare and useful disclosure that tells readers where the argument is soft.
- The institutional and historical framing is well sourced and hard to find elsewhere in one place: the WIOA accountability turn (Cherewka & Prins 2023; Condelli 2013), professionalization (Smith 2017), the funding formula's 88/12 split (Collins 2014), and the long history (Knowles 1994). This section is a legitimately useful reference for readers new to the sector.
- Novelty claims are modest and mostly accurate. The paper does not oversell; the Discussion explicitly says this 'is not a comprehensive exploration of all potential explanations.'

**Weaknesses:**

- The most consequential omission: no engagement with the immigration-enforcement and 'chilling effects' literature (e.g., Watson's work on immigration enforcement and Medicaid take-up; research on Secure Communities and safety-net participation; the public charge rule literature). This is a direct demand-side rival to the paper's supply-side conclusion — LEP adults may be avoiding public institutions rather than being turned away — and the paper's own framework would classify it under CostsD or the unmeasured alpha-D term. Because the paper concludes 'unmet demand' from provider capacity constraints (Cronen et al. 2023) plus anecdote, this gap matters for how much weight the conclusion can bear.
- One-sided treatment of the immigration-and-public-goods evidence. The claim that 'increases in immigration reduce spending on K–12 education and other social services' is supported by three sources that do not cleanly support it: Lanford & Quadagno (2022) is about Medicaid eligibility rules, not K–12 spending; Speciale (2012) is quasi-experimental evidence from Spain; Mayda et al. is an unpublished Bank of Canada working paper. Absent entirely is the contested side of this literature — the diversity-and-public-goods replication debate, Hopkins's finding that immigration provokes opposition only under specific salience conditions, and the sizable body of null or positive contact-effect results. Readers should not take this as a settled finding.
- Hainmueller & Hopkins's Annual Review of Political Science synthesis on public attitudes toward immigration is not cited. Its absence is notable in a paper that runs an immigration-framing survey experiment, since that synthesis's central claim — that opposition is sociotropic and cultural rather than fiscal self-interest — bears directly on how the paper's treatment effect should be interpreted (as a symbolic-threat prime, not a revealed preference over spending).
- The GED/high-school-equivalency literature is thin where the paper leans on it. The 43% decline in the ABE/ASE target population is attributed to graduation-rate improvements and 'reduced participation in HSE exams,' sourced to a Hechinger Report piece (Barshay 2018), Murnane (2013), and two of the first author's own unrefereed EdWorkingPapers (Heller 2024, 2025). The canonical work on GED returns and signaling — Cameron & Heckman; Tyler, Murnane & Willett; Heckman, Humphries & Kautz; Jepsen, Mueser & Troske — is absent, as is the specific literature on the 2014 GED redesign (harder, computerized, more expensive, plus the HiSET/TASC market split), which is a well-documented supply-side shock to HSE test-taking distinct from anything in the paper's model.
- The 'target population' construct is defined by credential attainment and English proficiency without engaging the adult-skills measurement literature that contradicts it. PIAAC evidence indicates a very large population of credentialed U.S. adults with low literacy and numeracy — the paper cites Hanushek et al. (2015) only in a footnote and never confronts the implication that its ABE/ASE 'target population' understates need, making the 43% decline partly an artifact of the proxy. Footnote 4 gestures at this but the literature that would sharpen it is not brought in.
- The evidence for the returns to adult ESL — described in the Discussion as 'especially robust' — rests on three studies, all Massachusetts/Greater Boston, one of them the authors' own (Heller & Slungaard Mumma 2023, AEJ:Policy) and two of them non-peer-reviewed reports (Roder & Elliott 2020, Economic Mobility Corp; Modestino et al. 2019, Boston Foundation). The geographic concentration and the gray-literature status are never flagged.
- Very little engagement with the qualitative and critical traditions in adult literacy education. Pickard (2022) — which posed the enrollment-decline question first, in Adult Literacy Education — is cited mainly as a data source for Figure 1 rather than engaged as the paper's closest antecedent. Practitioner-side accounts of how WIOA accountability reshaped who programs enroll are absent.
- The accountability-and-cost argument stops short of its own strongest implication. The paper cites Condelli (2013) and Cronen et al. (2023) on administrative burden but not the workforce-program performance-measurement literature (Heckman, Heinrich & Smith on JTPA; Courty & Marschke on gaming performance standards), which would raise a competing supply-side story: that accountability changed program composition and reporting incentives — recall NRS counts only participants reaching 12+ contact hours — rather than simply raising costs.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before repeating the sentence 'increases in immigration reduce spending on K–12 education and other social services,' check the three cited sources against the claim. Lanford & Quadagno (2022) concerns Medicaid eligibility, Speciale (2012) is Spanish quasi-experimental evidence, and Mayda, Senses & Steingress is an unpublished central-bank working paper (dated 2022 in text, 2023 in the reference list — one of them is wrong). None establishes the K–12 spending claim for the U.S. as stated.
- Read this paper alongside the immigration-enforcement chilling-effects literature — Watson on enforcement and Medicaid take-up, Alsan & Yang on Secure Communities and safety-net participation, and the public charge rule research. That work supplies the demand-side explanation the paper does not test, and it predicts the same observed pattern (growing LEP population, falling adult ESL enrollment) through an entirely different mechanism. The paper's supply-side conclusion is compatible with the data but not uniquely identified by it.
- Pair the deservingness framing with Hainmueller & Hopkins's Annual Review synthesis on public attitudes toward immigration and with Hopkins's work on when immigration becomes locally salient. Both qualify the paper's implicit model, and Coppock, Leeper & Mullinix (PNAS) on the generalizability of online survey experiments would actually strengthen — not undercut — the authors' own caveat that their CloudResearch convenience sample is unrepresentative.
- For the HSE side of the story, go to the primary literature rather than the paper's citations: Cameron & Heckman on GED nonequivalence, Tyler/Murnane/Willett and Jepsen/Mueser/Troske on GED earnings returns, Heckman, Humphries & Kautz on signaling, plus the research on the 2014 GED redesign and the HiSET/TASC market fragmentation. The paper's Heller (2024, 2025) citations are the first author's own unrefereed EdWorkingPapers and should be read as preprints.
- Cite Pickard (2022, Adult Literacy Education) as the antecedent that first framed the federally-funded adult education enrollment decline as a question for the field. This paper's distinctive contribution is not noticing the decline — it is decomposing it into supply and demand components and linking the immigrant-composition shift to funding through both a state panel and an experiment. Attribute accordingly.
- Treat the adult ESL returns evidence as promising but geographically narrow. All three cited studies (Heller & Slungaard Mumma 2023; Roder & Elliott 2020; Modestino et al. 2019) are Massachusetts/Boston, two are non-peer-reviewed, and one is by these authors. The 6% internal rate of return figure originates in the authors' own cost-benefit analysis and should be cited to that paper, not to this one, and with its single-program provenance attached.
- When using the paper's ABE/ASE 'target population' series, note that it is defined by credential status alone. Cross-reference PIAAC adult literacy and numeracy results, which suggest a substantially larger low-skill adult population than the no-diploma count captures — meaning the 43% decline in 'need' is partly a measurement artifact and the paper's own footnote 4 concedes the limitation.
- Two small citation cleanups worth catching before you copy references: Roder & Elliott's surname is spelled 'Elliot' in the body text and 'Elliott' in the reference list, and Gilens's Why Americans Hate Welfare was originally published in 1999 (the 2009 date is a later edition).

**Detailed Commentary:**

Overall assessment for readers: this is a well-built short synthesis whose citation practice is honest — the paper does not claim more than it shows, hedges where it should, and correctly labels its regression results as correlational. The literature review is efficient rather than exhaustive, which is appropriate for Educational Researcher's feature format. What readers should watch is not misrepresentation but asymmetry: the works cited are consistently those that support the deservingness mechanism, and the literatures that would complicate it are simply absent rather than dismissed.

On placement in the field: the paper sits at the intersection of three literatures and contributes unevenly to each. To the adult education literature it contributes real value — the assembled NRS record of the ABE/ASE-to-ESL composition reversal, the supply/demand decomposition, and the observation that the federal funding formula's 88% weight on uncredentialed adults mechanically penalizes states whose K–12 systems improve. That last point is a genuinely novel and citable institutional insight, and it is the paper's most durable contribution. To the deservingness and redistribution literature the contribution is thinner: a single-vignette framing experiment on a convenience sample of 1,000, finding effects concentrated among Republican respondents, is a competent replication of a well-established pattern (Alesina et al. 2023; Ellis & Faricy 2020) in a new policy domain rather than a theoretical advance. To the immigration-and-public-goods literature it adds a state panel with 292–725 observations whose key coefficient is null in the full period and significant only in truncated windows chosen partly on data-quality grounds — readers should weight this accordingly and not cite it as independent confirmation of the cross-national findings.

The engagement-with-conflicting-evidence dimension is where I'd flag the most caution. The paper reports its own null result honestly (Columns 1 and 4, both p > .5) but frames it as a data-quality issue rather than as evidence against the hypothesis, and the surrounding literature review offers readers no external benchmark for how contested this relationship is. A reader who knows only what this paper cites would come away believing the immigration–public goods link is settled. It is not. The replication disputes around ethnic diversity and public goods provision, the salience-conditional findings, and the null contact-effect results are all part of the evidence base a reader should hold alongside this paper.

On what to rely on versus treat cautiously: rely on the descriptive trends (Figures 1 and 2), the institutional description of WIOA funding, the documented decline in real spending, the near-doubling of real per-participant cost, and the administrator- and volunteer-ratio evidence — these are drawn directly from NRS and IES tables and are the paper's most solid material. Treat cautiously the inference that public willingness to spend is the operative channel connecting immigrant share to funding levels, and the characterization of the returns evidence as 'especially robust.'

I hold moderate confidence. I know the political economy, immigration attitudes, and economics-of-education literatures well enough to be confident about the specific omissions I've named. Adult literacy education as a specialized field — particularly its qualitative and practitioner scholarship, which appears in venues like Adult Education Quarterly, Adult Literacy Education, and Journal of Research and Practice for Adult Literacy — I know less well, so my judgment that the paper underengages that tradition is the part of this assessment a specialist should check.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The prose is clear, well-paced, and unusually well-signposted at the paragraph level: the supply/demand framing, the three numbered hypotheses, and the descriptive figures make the argument easy to follow, and most of the many numbers in the text reconcile exactly with Figures 1, 2a, 2b, and 3. But the paper carries a small number of consequential text-vs-exhibit failures — a cost figure (+98%) that cannot be reconciled with the paper's own spending and enrollment numbers, a factually wrong enrollment-rate claim in the Discussion's opening sentence, a significance level in the text that contradicts Table 1's own stars, and a 'unaffected' characterization that Figure 3's point estimates do not support — plus abstract language that is more causal and more definitive than the body. Readers can trust the descriptive architecture but should verify specific numbers before quoting them.

**Strengths:**

- Excellent macro-organization for a Feature Article: the supply/demand model (Equations 1-3) generates three explicitly numbered hypotheses, each gets its own subsection, and each subsection ends with a one-sentence verdict ('In summary, we find...'). A reader can reconstruct the entire argument from the headings and the summary sentences.
- The descriptive core is numerically sound. I checked the text against the exhibits and the H1 numbers all hold: Figure 2a shows the ABE/ASE target population at ~24.0M vs. LEP at ~16.6M in 2000 (the stated 7.4M gap), falling 43% and rising ~50% respectively by 2023; Figure 2b shows total enrollment 2.64M -> 1.27M (-52%), ABE/ASE -66%, ESL -33%, and an ESL enrollment share moving from ~43% to ~60% — every one of these matches the prose.
- Figure 2 is a genuinely well-built exhibit and does the paper's central expository work: stacking target populations (panel a) directly above enrollment (panel b) on a shared year axis makes the paper's motivating fact — a growing ESL target population alongside falling ESL enrollment — visible in a single glance. It is self-contained and the 'reversal' claim is verifiable from it.
- The paper is admirably explicit about its own limits in the body: it labels Table 1 'correlational (not causal),' states plainly that the survey sample 'is not representative of the U.S. population,' reports the 21-word Simmons et al. disclosure with preregistration and ResearchBox links, and concedes 'we cannot prove that these policy forces have increased costs.' These hedges are placed where the claims are made, not buried.
- Footnotes are used well rather than as a dumping ground — Note 3 in particular supplies the enrollment-as-share-of-target-population figures (ABE/ASE 6.3%->3.7%, ESL 6.8%->3.0%) that let a reader normalize the headline declines, and these too reconcile with Figure 2.
- Figure 3 reports exact means on every bar (.652/.579, .805/.810, .483/.314, .699/.622, etc.) and uses full 0-1 axes with no truncation, so the reader can audit the text's effect sizes directly rather than eyeballing bar heights.

**Weaknesses:**

- LOAD-BEARING ARITHMETIC INCONSISTENCY IN THE COST CLAIM (Hypothesis 3, p. 6). The text states real adult education spending fell 30% from 2005 to 2019, and separately that per-participant spending rose from 'approximately \$1,065 in 2019 dollars' (2005) to \$2,105 (2019), 'meaning real costs nearly doubled from 2005 to 2019 (+98%).' These cannot both be true given the paper's own Figure 2b, which shows enrollment falling from ~2.42M (2005) to ~1.11M (2019), i.e. -54%. A 30% spending decline against a 54% enrollment decline implies per-participant spending rose ~52%, not 98%. Multiplying out: \$1,065 x 2.42M = \$2.58B and \$2,105 x 1.11M = \$2.34B, i.e. a 9% total decline, not 30%. Consistency is restored only if the \$1,065 is a NOMINAL 2005 figure (~\$1,380 in 2019 dollars) despite being labeled '2019 dollars' — in which case the real increase is roughly +52% and the headline '+98%' / 'nearly doubled' is roughly double the true value. This is not a stray statistic: 'rising costs' is one of the two supply-side mechanisms in the abstract and the whole of Hypothesis 3.
- FACTUALLY WRONG CLAIM IN THE DISCUSSION'S OPENING SENTENCE (p. 9). 'Federally funded adult education programs once represented a substantial investment... with enrollment rates exceeding 1 in 100 adults in 2000. Today, that share is closer to 1 in 1,000 in absolute terms.' With 2023 enrollment of ~1.27M against ~262M U.S. adults, the rate is ~0.48%, or about 1 in 210 — roughly five times the stated figure. It also contradicts the paper's own Introduction, which says that even at the 2020 nadir (~700,000) enrollment was 'under 0.3% of U.S. adults' (~1 in 350). This is the most quotable sentence in the Discussion and it is wrong.
- TEXT-TABLE SIGNIFICANCE MISMATCH (p. 8 vs. Table 1). The text says a 1pp increase in the LEP share 'is associated with a 1.8% to 2.1% decrease in state funding for adult education (both ps < .01).' Table 1 reports Model 2 as -.021** and Model 3 as -.018*, and the table key is '*p < .05. **p < .01' — so by the table's own notation Model 3 is p < .05, not p < .01. (The reported -.018 with SE .006 gives t = 3.0, which would in fact merit **, so the error is likely in the star rather than the text — but the reader has no way to know which, and the two published statements disagree.)
- PROSE OUTRUNS FIGURE 3 ON POLITICAL INDEPENDENTS. The text says the treatment effect is 'driven by changes in the preferences of self-identified Republican respondents' and that 'Democrats or political independents are unaffected by their treatment assignment (both ps > .2).' Figure 3 shows independents moving from .699 to .622 on 'support increase' (-7.7pp) and from .049 to .122 on 'support decrease' (+7.3pp) — point estimates as large as or larger than the pooled effects the paper headlines (-7.2pp and +7.4pp). Only Democrats are genuinely flat (.805 -> .810). 'Unaffected' describes a p-value from n = 201, not the estimate; a reader who reads only the prose will carry away a sharper partisan story than the exhibit supports.
- ABSTRACT OVERSTATES AND MISDESCRIBES THE REGRESSOR. (a) Causal verb: 'the increasing immigrant share of adult education enrollments HAS DECREASED public willingness to invest' — the body explicitly calls Table 1 'correlational (not causal).' (b) Wrong quantity: the regression predictor is ShareLEP, 'the share of the TARGET POPULATION for adult education services in a state that is composed of potential adult ESL participants' — not the immigrant share of enrollments. (c) 'We rule out changes in aggregate demand as a primary driver' is stronger than the body's own conclusion ('cannot be explained by falling (aggregate) demand, although differences exist across program types'). (d) The abstract omits that the regression is null over the full 2005-2019 panel (Columns 1 and 4, both p > .5) and becomes significant only in two shorter windows chosen after the authors 'notice unusual patterns of year-to-year spending' — a specification dependence that materially conditions the finding.
- HYPOTHESIS 2 — THE PAPER'S CENTRAL SUPPLY-SIDE CLAIM — HAS NO IN-TEXT EXHIBIT. The entire funding-decline section (p. 6) is six sentences of prose ('The data support this hypothesis. Overall, real spending on adult education fell by 30%...') pointing to Online Appendix Figures B1 and B2. Likewise the returns-to-skills evidence for H1 lives entirely in Online Appendix A. A reader of the published article cannot see the funding trend that the abstract's 'constraining supply' rests on. The three visible exhibits document background (Figure 1), demand (Figure 2), and the deservingness mechanism (Table 1, Figure 3); the supply claim itself is invisible.
- FIGURE 1 CONTAINS A DISCONTINUITY THE TEXT NEVER MENTIONS. Total enrollment sits at ~4.05M in 1995-1997 and then falls to ~3.62M (1998), ~2.89M (1999), and ~2.65M (2000) — a ~35% collapse in three years, the steepest decline anywhere in the 60-year series, immediately before the study window opens. The text writes 'Enrollment in adult education programs decreased dramatically in the following years... as shown in Figure 1,' which points at the figure while passing over the fact that the figure's most dramatic decrease precedes the baseline. Nothing in the prose or the figure note tells the reader whether this is a real decline or an NRS reporting/definitional change, and it bears directly on whether 2000 is a clean starting point.
- H3'S EVIDENCE IS PARTLY DEFINITIONAL AND THE PROSE DOESN'T SAY SO. Per-participant cost is spending divided by enrollment, so a large enrollment decline mechanically raises it. The section presents that ratio as evidence that 'rising costs have limited the reach of spending,' and the concluding sentence ('Rising costs have exacerbated reductions in resources imposed by falling funding') reads as an independent finding. The supporting evidence that is genuinely independent — the administrator ratio (206 -> 106 participants per administrator, which does check out: 2.67M/12,963 and ~1.26M/11,864) and the volunteer share (>30% -> <13%) — is offered as suggestive, but the summary sentence does not carry that qualification forward.
- NAVIGATION IS HURT BY REPEATED AND MIS-LEVELED HEADINGS. The article has three separate top-level 'Results' headings (p. 5 for H1-H3, p. 8 for the regression, p. 9 for the survey experiment), so a reader scanning the PDF cannot tell from a heading which results they are in. 'Regression Analysis' and 'Survey Experiment' are typeset at the same level as 'Explaining Declines in Public Funding' even though they are logically its subsections. 'Data' appears before the conceptual model, and Part 1 has no methods section at all.
- PRODUCTION ERRORS THAT SURVIVED COPYEDITING. The section heading on p. 5 reads 'Conceputal Models' (misspelled). On p. 8 the text says 'Equation 1 also includes vectors of state and year fixed effects' — it means Equation 5. P. 2: 'we consider potential explanations adult education's 21st-century decline' (missing 'for'). Notation shifts from ShareLEP_st in Equation 5 to LEPshare_st two paragraphs later. Table 1's note has an unclosed parenthesis. Citation mismatches: text 'Mayda et al., 2022' vs. reference list Mayda et al. (2023); text 'Roder and Elliot (2020)' vs. reference 'Roder, A., & Elliott, M.' Also note the dollar base year changes without comment — Table 1 is in real 2024\$ while the cost discussion is in 2019\$.
- FIGURE 3'S ERROR BARS ARE ONE-SIDED. The note says 'Error bars report the 95% confidence interval of the treatment group mean' — and indeed only the treatment bars carry them. The control means (also ~n=500 each) are drawn as bare bars, which visually presents them as fixed reference points and prevents a reader from assessing any difference by eye. Panel B compounds this: on a 0-1 axis, values of .01 to .232 are nearly unreadable, so the outcome with the largest relative treatment effect (+148%) is the one the reader can least see.
- MINOR ROUNDING SLIPPAGE IN THE SURVEY RESULTS. The text reports a 7.2pp reduction in support for increasing funding, but Figure 3A gives .652 - .579 = 7.3pp; and a 7.4pp increase in support for decreasing funding, but Figure 3B gives .125 - .050 = 7.5pp. Both are consistent with rounding in the underlying means, but a reader recomputing from the figure will not land on the text's numbers. Relatedly, 'driven by... Republican respondents (all ps < .005)' is ambiguous: Figure 3C shows Republican 'support maintain' moving only .429 -> .454, which cannot be p < .005, so 'all' must mean 'the two outcomes just discussed.'

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read Figure 2 (both panels) closely — it is the paper's best exhibit and the entire Hypothesis 1 argument rests on it. I verified every number the text draws from it and they all hold, so you can quote the demand-side descriptive claims (43% decline in the ABE/ASE target population, ~50% growth in the LEP target population, -52% total enrollment, -67% ABE/ASE, -33% ESL, 42% -> 60% ESL share) with confidence.
- Do NOT cite the '+98%' / 'real costs nearly doubled' figure or the '\$1,065 in 2019 dollars' 2005 baseline without going to the underlying NCES tables (IES 2008 and 2023a). Cross-multiplied against the paper's own -30% real spending decline and Figure 2b's enrollment path, the implied real per-participant increase is roughly +50%, not +98%. If you need the cost-growth fact, cite the direction and the administrator/volunteer evidence, not the magnitude.
- Ignore the Discussion's opening 'closer to 1 in 1,000' sentence. Use the Introduction's figures instead: ~1.3% of U.S. adults in 2000, under 0.3% at the 2020 nadir, and roughly 0.5% (about 1 in 200) today.
- When citing Table 1, read the coefficients and stars directly rather than the surrounding paragraph. The full-panel models (Columns 1 and 4) are null; the significant results come only from the 2011-2019 and 2014-2019 windows; and the text's 'both ps < .01' for Columns 2 and 3 disagrees with the single asterisk on Model 3. Also describe the predictor accurately as the LEP share of the state's TARGET POPULATION, not the immigrant share of enrollments as the abstract has it.
- Table 1 also contains two rows the Results text never discusses: ln(Target population of nongraduate, non-LEP adults) is .496* in Model 5, .218 (ns) in Model 6, and wrong-signed at -.129 in Model 4. Since the paper's stated prediction was that this coefficient would be positive, look at these rows yourself before characterizing how well the pattern matched expectations.
- Before repeating the 'Republicans drive the effect' framing, look at the Independent bars in Figure 3 panels A and B (.699 -> .622 and .049 -> .122). The point estimates are comparable to the pooled effects; the 'unaffected' language reflects n = 201 and wide CIs, not a null estimate. The Democrat null (.805 -> .810) is the only clean one.
- If the funding-decline claim matters to your use of this paper, you must open Online Appendix Figures B1 and B2 — there is no in-text exhibit for Hypothesis 2, and the same goes for Online Appendix A if you need the returns-to-skills evidence and Appendix C for the survey design and balance.
- Look at the left third of Figure 1 before treating 2000 as a natural baseline: total enrollment falls from ~4.05M (1997) to ~2.65M (2000), the steepest drop in the whole 60-year series, and the paper does not discuss it or say whether it reflects an NRS reporting change.
- Skimmable without loss: the five short covariate subsections on p. 8 (Potential Beneficiaries, Population, Economic Conditions, Politics, Other Costs) — Table 1's note lists the same controls more compactly; the historical background under 'Adult Education in the United States' (though the federal formula detail — 88% uncredentialed adults / 12% immigrants — is the setup for the policy recommendation on p. 11, so read that one paragraph); and the two paragraphs of Welfare-to-Work/LSAL literature on pp. 3-4.
- Must-not-skip for a careful reader: pp. 5-6 (the H1-H3 verdicts, where the interpretive work happens), the last paragraph of the 'Models' section on p. 7 (which is where 'public willingness to spend' enters the framework as an unmeasured factor whose absence the ShareLEP coefficient is asked to stand in for), and Figure 3 with its exact printed means.
- Treat the abstract as a summary of the authors' interpretation rather than of the evidence: it uses a causal verb for results the body labels correlational, says 'rule out' where the body says 'cannot be explained by,' and omits both the full-panel null and the fact that the experiment is a 1,000-person non-representative convenience sample measuring stated funding preferences.

**Detailed Commentary:**

I read the full extracted text and inspected all four exhibits in the PDF at high resolution, including cropped enlargements of Figures 1, 2a, and 2b to read individual data points. The rating of 'adequate' rather than 'strong' turns almost entirely on fidelity rather than craft: sentence by sentence and section by section this is a well-made, readable article, and the great majority of the numbers I could check reconciled exactly.

What reconciles (worth stating, because it means most of the paper is quotable as written): the 2000 baseline of 2.67M and the 42%/60% ESL enrollment shares against Figure 2b (1.13/2.64 = 43%; 0.76/1.27 = 60%); the -52%, -67%, and -33% enrollment declines; the 7.4M target-population gap in 2000 against Figure 2a (24.0M vs. 16.6M); the <5% total target decline (40.5M -> 38.6M); the '1.25 million additional participants' counterfactual, which I reproduced to within rounding; footnote 3's 6.3%->3.7% and 6.8%->3.0% participation rates; the administrator arithmetic (2.67M/12,963 = 206; ~1.26M/11,864 = 106; an 8.5% decline in administrators); the \$2,105 vs. \$13,496 vs. \$9,349 sector comparisons; every survey mean quoted in the text against the printed values in Figure 3; the internal consistency of the -7.2pp/-11% and +7.4pp/+148% pairs; and the plausibility of the Republican effect size (-16.9pp on ~200 per arm) as the driver of a -7.2pp pooled effect given a 40% Republican sample. Colorado's exclusion (states = 49) matches the Table 1 note and the observation counts are close to the implied cell counts. This is a paper whose author-team clearly checked its own arithmetic in most places.

Against that background, the failures stand out sharply and are concentrated in exactly the places a reader is most likely to quote. The cost inconsistency is the most serious because it is not a typo but a claim that cannot be true alongside two other claims in the same paper, and it is one of the two supply-side mechanisms in the abstract. The Discussion's '1 in 1,000' error is the most likely to propagate, because it is the opening sentence of the Discussion and it self-contradicts the Introduction by a factor of five. The Table 1 star/text disagreement and the 'unaffected' characterization of independents are smaller but both push in the same direction — toward a reader coming away more confident in the deservingness result than the exhibits warrant.

On abstract fidelity specifically: a reader who stops at the abstract will believe (i) that aggregate demand has been ruled out, (ii) that a causal relationship between immigrant share of ENROLLMENTS and public willingness to invest has been demonstrated, and (iii) that this holds generally. The body supports something narrower on all three counts — a descriptive case against the demand explanation, a correlational association between the LEP share of the TARGET POPULATION and state funding that appears only in post-2011 subsamples selected after inspecting the data, and a stated-preference experiment in a self-described non-representative convenience sample. The gap between abstract and body here is larger than the gap between body and exhibits.

On structure: the two-part design ('why did enrollment fall' then 'why did funding fall') is a good choice and is announced clearly in the Introduction. The costs are the repeated 'Results' headings, the mis-leveled 'Regression Analysis'/'Survey Experiment' heads, and the offloading of Hypothesis 2's entire evidentiary basis to an online appendix — which for a Feature Article in a journal read partly for its accessible synthesis is a real cost to the reader, not a formatting quibble.

My confidence is held at 0.85 rather than higher because I could not access the online appendices (A, B including Figures B1/B2 and Table B2, and C). Those hold the funding trend series, the returns-to-skills estimation, the control-variable definitions, the weighted regressions, and the full survey instrument and balance checks — a substantial share of the paper's load-bearing material, and the place where the cost/spending discrepancy I flag might (or might not) be resolved.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This paper assembles the clearest available account of why U.S. public adult education enrollment halved between 2000 and 2023, arguing the decline is a supply-side story (falling real funding plus per-participant costs that nearly doubled) rather than a demand-side one, and layering on a political-economy hypothesis that the sector's shift toward immigrant ESL beneficiaries eroded public willingness to fund it. Its durable contribution is descriptive and framing-level: the documented reversal in target populations (ABE/ASE target down 43% while the LEP target grew ~50%, crossing over in 2007) alongside a 33% drop in ESL enrollment is a genuinely useful reframing of the decline as unmet need. The political-economy claim, which is the paper's most quotable, rests on a fragile state panel and a non-representative vignette experiment, and is best read as a well-motivated hypothesis with suggestive support rather than an established finding.

**Strengths:**

- The target-population decomposition is the paper's real analytic insight and is new: prior work (Pickard, 2022) documented the enrollment decline, but this paper is the first to show that the decline is entirely inconsistent with need — the ESL target population grew ~50% while ESL enrollment fell 33%, and the two target populations crossed over in 2007. That reversal figure (Figure 2a) reframes a story previously read as 'demand dried up' into one about rationed supply.
- Careful, well-sourced quantification of the sector's fiscal anatomy from NRS, IPUMS, and NCES: real total spending down 30% and state spending down 35% (2005–2019), real per-participant spending up 98% from ~\$1,065 to \$2,105, and benchmarking against \$13,496 K–12 per-pupil spending. These figures are assembled from scattered federal sources and are the numbers the field currently lacks a single citable home for.
- The paper does real work to rule out the leading alternative explanation rather than assuming it away: it shows the aggregate target population shrank <5%, and it estimates (via ACS Mincerian models) that real returns to both an HSE credential and English proficiency rose over the period — the opposite of what a demand-decline story predicts.
- First application of the deservingness / in-group literature (Alesina, Luttmer, Ellis & Faricy, Van Oorschot) to adult education, a sector where the compositional shift is unusually stark and the theory therefore has unusual bite. This is a genuine cross-literature bridge, not a repackaging.
- The survey experiment is transparently and credibly executed on its own terms: preregistered on AsPredicted, materials/data/code on ResearchBox, an active control (citizen beneficiaries) rather than a no-information control, and a 21-word-solution disclosure. The heterogeneity result — the entire effect loading on Republicans, whose support for increases falls from 48.3% to 31.4% while Democrats and independents are unmoved — is more informative than the pooled average and is the paper's cleanest new evidence.
- The authors are unusually candid about their own limits: they label the regressions correlational, disclaim national generalizability for the survey, concede they 'cannot prove' the cost mechanisms, and acknowledge unmeasured demand-side substitutes. The paper's boundaries are drawn honestly in the body even where the abstract runs ahead of them.

**Weaknesses:**

- The abstract's causal chain — rising immigrant share → lower public willingness to invest → constrained supply → unmet demand — is assembled from four separate pieces of evidence, none of which identifies the link it is asked to carry, and the joints between them are never tested. Readers will encounter this as a finding; it is a synthesis of suggestive parts.
- The state-panel result is the paper's most fragile element and is presented in a way that understates that fragility. The coefficient on LEP share is null over the full 2005–2019 panel (Models 1 and 4, both p > .5) and becomes significant only in two shorter windows chosen after the authors noticed 'unusual patterns' in early years. With 50 states, a multiply-determined autocorrelated outcome, and one large idiosyncratic shock (California's post-recession collapse) sitting in exactly the excluded early period, the difference between the null and the significant estimates is not clearly a data-quality story rather than a specification-search one. The sign on ln(nongraduate population) is also positive and significant in only one of three columns, weakening the intended placebo-style contrast.
- The survey experiment identifies the effect of making immigrant beneficiaries salient in a one-sentence description, not the effect of actual demographic change on legislative appropriations. It is an internally valid framing experiment being asked to stand in for a fifteen-year political process; nothing in the design connects stated preferences of 1,000 online respondents to state budget outcomes.
- Timing is a live external-validity threat the paper does not confront: the experiment was fielded May 29–June 3, 2025, during an extraordinary peak in immigration salience and enforcement. The authors argue only that they see no reason for survey-pool selection to bias results directionally — which addresses sample composition, not the period effect. A 7.2-point framing effect measured in that window may not characterize the 2005–2019 period the funding analysis covers.
- The demand-side ruling-out is less complete than the abstract's 'we rule out changes in aggregate demand' implies. Free, high-quality private substitutes for adult ESL (Duolingo and comparable tools, YouTube, online courses) grew from nothing to mass adoption over precisely this window, and the paper dismisses this in a single sentence as unmeasurable. For ESL specifically — the service carrying the paper's argument — this is a plausible competing explanation for falling enrollment against a growing target population.
- Immigration enforcement and chilling effects are absent from the demand analysis despite being an obvious candidate: LEP immigrants' willingness to enroll in a federally reported program with individual-level data collection plausibly fell after 2016, which would depress ESL enrollment through demand, not supply. This omission matters because it would produce the same observed pattern the paper attributes to funding constraints.
- The evidence for unmet demand — the claim doing the most policy work — is thin: one 2018 provider survey (29% of ESL programs turning students away) plus anecdote and news reports. There is no waitlist series, no measure of how the turn-away rate changed over the study period, and therefore no direct evidence that rationing intensified as enrollment fell.
- Hypotheses 2 and 3 are descriptive accounting rather than tests. That funding fell and per-participant costs rose is measurement; the attribution of cost growth to accountability burden, professionalization, and Baumol effects is asserted from suggestive correlates (administrator ratios, volunteer share) that the authors themselves call 'likely candidates.' The paper's own framing invites readers to treat these as established mechanisms.
- The ABE/ASE side of the story is under-developed relative to its size. ABE/ASE enrollment fell 67% against a 43% target-population decline, and the 2014 GED overhaul (computerization, price increases, competing HSE exams) is a well-known sector-specific shock relegated to citations of the lead author's own working papers rather than analyzed. Roughly 40% of the sector's decline is thus explained mostly by reference elsewhere.
- The authors' own prior randomized evaluation (Heller & Slungaard Mumma, 2023) supplies the returns evidence underwriting the policy recommendation to expand adult ESL. That is legitimate, but readers should note the paper's central normative claim rests substantially on the authors' own single-program Massachusetts study rather than an independent body of evidence.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR the descriptive anatomy of the decline — enrollment falling from 2.67 million (about 1.3% of adults) in 2000 to under 1.3 million by 2023, the ESL share rising from 42% to 60%, real total spending down 30% and state spending down 35% (2005–2019), and real per-participant spending nearly doubling to \$2,105. These are the paper's best-supported and most durable claims, carefully compiled from NRS/IPUMS/NCES, and this is now the single best citable source for them.
- CITE IT FOR the target-population reversal and the resulting mismatch: the ABE/ASE target population fell 43% while the LEP target grew ~50%, crossing in 2007, yet ESL enrollment fell 33%. This is the paper's genuine analytic contribution and the strongest basis for the claim that adult ESL supply is rationed relative to need.
- CITE IT FOR the experimental finding that describing adult education beneficiaries as immigrants rather than as citizens seeking an HSE credential reduces stated support for funding, with the effect concentrated among Republican respondents. State it as a framing/salience effect in a convenience sample — that is exactly what was identified, and it is cleanly identified.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT for the claim that anti-immigrant sentiment caused the decline in adult education funding. The state panel is correlational, null in its fullest specification, and significant only in post hoc sub-periods; the experiment measures stated preferences, not appropriations. This is the paper's most quotable claim and its least supported one — the gap between the two is the main hazard in citing this paper.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT for the strong reading that demand did not fall. The paper credibly rules out shrinking population and falling returns to skills, but it does not address free private ESL substitutes or immigration-enforcement chilling effects, either of which could depress ESL enrollment through demand while producing the pattern the paper attributes to supply.
- DO NOT CITE the regression coefficients (a 1.8–2.1% funding decrease per percentage-point rise in LEP share; a 0.31–0.32% decrease per 1% rise in the LEP target population) as effect sizes or as inputs to a policy calculation. They are within-state associations from a 50-state panel with a specification-dependent sign of significance.
- DO NOT CITE the survey magnitudes (7.2 points, 7.4 points, the 48.3%-to-31.4% Republican shift) as estimates of U.S. public opinion. The sample is a non-representative CloudResearch convenience panel — the authors say so explicitly — and the fielding window (late May 2025) was a period of unusually high immigration salience.
- USE IT AS a framing and agenda-setting piece for the political economy of demographically shifting social programs, including the generalization to K–12 and other immigrant-serving services. Treat that extension as a hypothesis the paper articulates well, not as something it tests.
- OPEN QUESTIONS a reader should know remain unresolved: whether the compositional shift actually moved legislative appropriations (as opposed to moving survey respondents); how much of the ESL enrollment decline is rationing versus substitution to free digital tools or enforcement-driven withdrawal; whether unmet demand actually grew over the period, which no time series currently establishes; what drove the near-doubling of per-participant costs, which is measured but not decomposed; and whether the political framing effect predates 2025 or is specific to the current moment.
- READ THE VENUE CORRECTLY: this is an Educational Researcher Feature Article — a synthesis-and-argument format, not a causal-identification venue. Judged as descriptive political economy that reframes a policy problem and motivates follow-on work, it succeeds; judged as evidence on the cause of the funding decline, it is a first word rather than a last one.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Standing in the literature. Before this paper, the decline in adult education enrollment was documented mainly in Pickard (2022) and scattered federal reports, and the political-economy literature on deservingness (Alesina & Glaeser; Luttmer; Ellis & Faricy; Van Oorschot; Lanford & Quadagno) had not been applied to this sector. The paper's contribution is to join those two literatures and to supply the descriptive scaffolding — target populations by service type, funding and cost series, composition shifts — that the field lacked. On the descriptive question ('what happened to adult education, and is it a need story or a resource story?') this is now the best available reference and will likely become the standard citation. On the causal question ('did immigrant composition cause the funding decline?') it is the first serious attempt, not the best available evidence, because there is not yet a body of evidence to be best within.

The gap between quotable and supported. This is the reader's-guide issue that matters most. The abstract closes with a fully causal sentence — the increasing immigrant share 'has decreased public willingness to invest as costs have risen, constraining supply and leading to unmet demand.' That is four causal links. Link one (composition shifted) is established. Link two (composition reduced willingness) is supported by a framing experiment and a specification-sensitive panel. Link three (reduced willingness reduced appropriations) is not tested at all — no mechanism connects public opinion to legislative outcomes anywhere in the paper. Link four (constrained supply produced unmet demand) rests on one 2018 provider survey. The body of the paper is appropriately hedged about each of these; the abstract and title are not. Papers get cited from their abstracts, and this one will be cited for a claim its own results section does not make.

On the regression specifically. The pattern deserves flagging plainly: the coefficient of interest is null with p > .5 in the specification using all 725 state-year observations, and becomes significant only after dropping to 431 and then 292 observations. The stated rationale — data-reporting discrepancies in early years, and the 2014 WIOA reauthorization tightening reporting — is plausible and was disclosed, which is to the authors' credit. But the excluded window also contains California's post-recession collapse, an idiosyncratic shock that moves the largest LEP state's funding for reasons orthogonal to deservingness politics, and the paper does not show whether the sub-period results survive dropping California or whether the full-period null is driven by it. Readers should treat these estimates as consistent with the hypothesis rather than as evidence for it, which is close to how the authors themselves frame it before pivoting to the experiment.

On generalizability. The paper draws its boundaries honestly in most places — it explicitly disclaims national representativeness for the survey and explicitly calls the analysis non-comprehensive. The one boundary it does not draw is temporal: an experiment fielded in the first week of June 2025 is used to illuminate funding dynamics from 2005 to 2019, and the possibility that the framing effect is far larger now than it was across the funding period is never raised. The extension to K–12 and other social services in the discussion is offered as speculation ('cautionary tale or bellwether') and should be read that way.

Bottom line for readers. Take the descriptive core — it is careful, well-sourced, and fills a real gap. Take the reframing of adult ESL as a rationed rather than a shrinking service — it is the paper's best idea and is reasonably supported. Take the survey experiment as a clean demonstration that beneficiary framing moves stated support among Republicans. Do not take the paper as having shown that immigration politics caused adult education's fiscal decline; that remains an open and important question the paper is valuable for having posed sharply.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper is built almost entirely on public data sources that are named with unusual precision — NRS aggregate reports, a versioned IPUMS USA citation with DOI, and NCES Digest tables cited by exact table number and URL — and the survey experiment half is exemplary: preregistered on AsPredicted with a live link, materials/data/code deposited at ResearchBox, verbatim treatment wording, and an explicit 21-word-solution disclosure. The archival half is weaker: there is no data availability statement or deposited replication package covering the panel regressions, no named deflator, and the construction of the LEP/target-population measures that drive both the descriptive figures and the key regressor is left to an online appendix the article body does not summarize. A determined replicator could rebuild most of this from public files, but would have to guess at several consequential definitional choices.

**Strengths:**

- Every data input is public and specifically cited rather than gestured at: NRS aggregate reports (https://nrs.ed.gov/rt/reports/aggregate), IPUMS USA cited as a versioned dataset with DOI (Ruggles et al. 2025, Version 16.0, https://doi.org/10.18128/D010.V16.0), and NCES Digest tables identified by exact table number (236.20, 236.55, 330.10, 179, 173) with URLs. This is materially better than the field norm of citing 'ACS data' or 'NCES.'
- The survey experiment meets modern open-science standards nearly in full: preregistration is publicly linked (aspredicted.org/rbhy-yr3n.pdf), materials, data, and code are deposited at researchbox.org/5571, the vendor (CloudResearch Connect) and exact fielding window (May 29–June 3, 2025) are named, N = 1,000 with subgroup ns reported in the Figure 3 note, and the paper carries the explicit Simmons et al. (2012) disclosure that sample-size determination, all exclusions, manipulations, and measures are reported.
- The experimental stimulus is reproducible from the article text alone: the neutral framing paragraph, the active-control sentence, and the immigrant-treatment sentence are all quoted verbatim, as is the outcome question, the 5-point Likert response set, and the exact rule for collapsing it into the binary 'support decreasing' and 'maintain' indicators.
- The panel specification is written out as an estimating equation with the estimand named, the full control vector enumerated in both text and the Table 1 note, state and year fixed effects stated, standard errors identified as cluster-robust at the state level, and the alternative log-population specification described alongside its predicted sign pattern.
- Sample-construction decisions that materially affect the results are disclosed rather than buried: the 2005 start (first year of state expenditure data), the omission of 2020+ for COVID disruption, the three analysis windows with a stated rationale for each, and the Colorado exclusion after 2009 documented in the Table 1 note.
- The paper is candid about the limits of its own inference — it labels Table 1 correlational, flags the small state panel and autocorrelated outcome, and explicitly disclaims generalizability of the convenience-sample experiment, which lets a reader calibrate trust without needing the underlying files.

**Weaknesses:**

- There is no data availability statement and no replication package covering the archival half of the paper. The ResearchBox and AsPredicted deposits are scoped to the experiment ('All experiments were preregistered... all preregistrations, materials, data, and code'), so the code that builds the state-year panel, constructs the target-population measures, and estimates Table 1 — the paper's headline quantitative result — appears not to be deposited anywhere. Under current journal norms this is the main gap.
- The operational definition of 'limited English proficient' is never given in the article body — only 'LEP adults regardless of educational attainment.' In IPUMS this requires a specific threshold on SPEAKENG (e.g., 'not at all' and 'not well' versus also including 'well'), and the choice directly scales both the Figure 2a crossover date and the ShareLEP regressor in every column of Table 1. The parallel ABE/ASE definition (English-proficient adults 18+ without a diploma or equivalent) is stated more clearly, but the EDUC/EDUCD coding of 'or equivalent credential' — whether GED holders are separable — is not.
- The IPUMS extract is otherwise unspecified in the text: sample series (ACS 1-year? which years?), weights (PERWT versus none), age and group-quarters restrictions, and how the year 2000 is handled at all, given that the ACS was not fully implemented until 2005. The 2000 figures presumably come from Census 2000 (the paper does separately cite Census 2000 Table P035), but the harmonization across the 2000–2004 gap that underpins the paper's signature '2000 to 2023' comparisons is not described.
- No price index is named anywhere, despite the paper's core claims being real-dollar changes: a 30% real spending decline, a 35% state decline, a 14% federal decline, a 98% real per-participant cost increase, and Table 1's outcome in 'real 2024\$' while per-participant figures are quoted in 2019 dollars. CPI-U, CPI-U-RS, PCE, and a state-and-local-government price deflator would give visibly different magnitudes for a 2005–2019 comparison.
- The Table 1 observation counts do not fully reconcile with the documented exclusions. Model 1 spans 2005–2019 across 50 states (750 possible state-years) and reports 725; Colorado dropping out after 2009 accounts for 10, leaving roughly 15 state-years missing with no explanation. Models 2 and 5 (2011–2019, 49 states = 441 possible) report 431, again about 10 unexplained. Whatever the reason — nonreporting states, suppressed cells — it is undocumented, and a replicator will not know whether their own panel matches.
- The reason for restricting to later windows is stated impressionistically ('we notice unusual patterns of year-to-year spending in the earlier years... which makes us concerned about data reporting discrepancies') without any documentation of which states or years were anomalous or what diagnostic was applied. This matters more than usual because the full-panel estimates in Columns 1 and 4 are null (both ps > .5) and only the restricted windows are significant, so the undocumented judgment call is precisely what separates a null from the paper's finding.
- The returns-to-skills analysis supporting the rejection of the falling-benefits channel is described in one sentence — a Mincer-style specification 'controlling for individual-level characteristics' — with no controls named, no sample restrictions, no income measure or top-code handling, and no point estimates in the body. The claim that returns 'increased modestly' between 2000 and 2023 is unverifiable from the article itself and rests entirely on Online Appendix A.
- The survey experiment's estimator is never stated. Effects are reported as percentage-point differences with p-values (7.2 pp, p = .021; 7.4 pp, p < .001) but with no standard errors or confidence intervals for the differences, no statement of whether estimates are raw differences in proportions or covariate-adjusted, and no indication of whether the by-party heterogeneity — which is the paper's interpretive payoff — was a preregistered primary analysis or exploratory, or whether any multiplicity adjustment was applied across the three party subgroups and multiple outcome codings.
- No software environment is reported: no statistical package or version, no packages, no random seed for any randomization or resampling. The randomization procedure itself (simple versus blocked, and on what, and whether balance was checked) is not described in the body.
- Several load-bearing descriptive statistics are secondhand from a single NCEE report (Cronen et al., 2023) — the 29%/12%/10% turn-away rates, the 64% 'very challenging' data-collection figure, the federal/state/local funding split — with no page or table references, so checking them means reading the source cover to cover.
- The specification section contains a cross-reference error, referring to fixed effects being included in 'Equation 1' when the estimating equation is Equation 5, which is a small but real obstacle to reading the specification unambiguously.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the survey-experiment results as the most verifiable claims in the paper. Before citing them, pull the ResearchBox deposit (researchbox.org/5571) and the preregistration (aspredicted.org/rbhy-yr3n.pdf) and check three things specifically: whether the by-party heterogeneity was preregistered as a primary analysis or is exploratory, whether the binary collapse of the 5-point outcome was the preregistered coding, and whether the reported N = 1,000 matches the number recruited (i.e., what the exclusions were). The Republican-subgroup result carries most of the paper's interpretive weight and is the one most worth confirming was planned.
- Do not cite the Table 1 magnitudes (the 1.8%–2.1% per percentage point, or the –0.31 to –0.32 elasticities) as settled without noting that the full-period estimates are null. The finding exists only in the 2011–2019 and 2014–2019 windows, and the rationale for excluding earlier years is a stated data-quality concern that the paper does not document. A reader relying on this result should ask the authors which state-years showed the anomalous reporting patterns and should regard the window choice as an open researcher-degrees-of-freedom question rather than a settled one.
- If you intend to rebuild the panel, request from the authors, or reconstruct and state explicitly, four definitional choices before you start: the SPEAKENG threshold defining LEP, the EDUC/EDUCD coding of 'no high school diploma or equivalent,' the weighting scheme for the IPUMS-derived population counts, and the price index used for real dollars. Each independently moves the ShareLEP regressor or the outcome, and none is recoverable from the article body. Online Appendix B is the first place to look; if it does not pin these down, they are guesses.
- Reconcile the Table 1 observation counts against your own panel as a first diagnostic. The gap of roughly 15 state-years in the 2005–2019 models and 10 in the 2011–2019 models beyond the documented Colorado exclusion is unexplained; if your reconstructed panel has a different N, that mismatch — not your coefficients — is the first thing to resolve.
- The descriptive backbone of the paper is the most directly checkable part and worth spot-verifying independently: the enrollment series, the ABE/ASE-to-adult-ESL composition shift (42% to 60%), the administrator and volunteer counts, and the entering-skill-level distributions all come from the public NRS aggregate reports at nrs.ed.gov, which anyone can query in an afternoon. If those reproduce, the paper's core factual claim about the scale and composition of the decline stands on its own regardless of the regression evidence.
- Treat the returns-to-skills conclusion — that the benefits channel can be ruled out — as taken on trust unless you read Online Appendix A. The body reports no estimates, no controls, and no sample definition for that analysis, so the rejection of Hypothesis 1's benefits mechanism is not independently checkable from the article.
- Note the deflator ambiguity when quoting the paper's real-dollar magnitudes. The 30% spending decline, 35% state decline, and 98% per-participant cost increase are all index-dependent over 2005–2019; report them as approximate and attribute the base year the paper used in each instance (2019 dollars for per-participant figures, 2024 dollars for Table 1) rather than mixing them.
- If your use requires an exact replication of Table 1, plan on corresponding with the authors for the panel-construction code. Given that the underlying inputs are all public and the experimental half was fully deposited, this is a reasonable request likely to succeed, but as published the regression half is a reconstruct-from-description exercise rather than a run-the-package one.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This paper sits at an interesting split. Its second half — the survey experiment — is close to a model of contemporary open-science practice: public preregistration with a resolvable link, a full deposit of materials, data, and code at a third-party repository, verbatim stimulus text in the article, an explicit disclosure statement, a named vendor and exact fielding dates, and an unusually honest paragraph about the convenience sample's non-representativeness. A reader can check essentially every step of that analysis. Its first half — the descriptive trends and the state panel regressions — is built on public data cited with real precision, but ships with no data availability statement and no deposited code, and pushes the variable-construction detail into online appendices that the body does not summarize even at a high level.

That asymmetry is what places this at 'adequate' rather than 'strong.' Nothing here is hidden or unverifiable in principle: NRS aggregate reports are freely downloadable, IPUMS is free with registration, and the NCES Digest tables are cited to the table number. Any competent replicator has access to every input. But access to inputs is not the same as reproducibility, and the distance between the two is measured in exactly the choices this paper leaves unstated in its body — the SPEAKENG cut defining LEP, the treatment of the pre-ACS years around 2000, the weighting, and the price index. Each of these is a defensible-either-way decision that shifts the reported quantities, and the paper's signature findings are all differences over long horizons where such choices compound.

The most consequential transparency gap is not a missing file but a missing diagnostic. The paper reports six models; the two estimated on the full 2005–2019 panel are null with p-values above .5, and the four estimated on truncated windows are significant. The justification for truncation is that the authors 'notice unusual patterns of year-to-year spending in the earlier years' and are 'concerned about data reporting discrepancies.' This is a legitimate concern and the authors deserve real credit for disclosing it rather than silently reporting only the preferred window. But disclosure without documentation leaves the reader unable to evaluate it: no list of anomalous states or years, no comparison of NRS-reported state expenditures against an independent source, no sensitivity analysis dropping the suspect observations from the full panel rather than dropping all early years for all states. A replicator working from the public NRS files could construct that diagnostic themselves, and I would encourage anyone leaning on Table 1 to do so, because it is the single check that would move this result from suggestive to solid.

A smaller but concrete signal of the same issue is the arithmetic of the observation counts. Fifteen years times fifty states is 750; Model 1 reports 725. Colorado's post-2009 nonreporting explains ten of the twenty-five. The remaining fifteen state-years are undocumented, as are roughly ten in the 2011–2019 models. This is not a serious threat to the findings, but it is the kind of thing that would be self-evident in a deposited build script and is instead invisible here — and it means a replicator whose panel comes out at 740 observations will not know whether they have made an error or the authors made a different, unstated exclusion.

On the experimental side, the main residual uncertainty is analytic rather than material. The article never names the estimator behind the 7.2- and 7.4-percentage-point effects, reports p-values without accompanying standard errors or confidence intervals for the differences themselves (Figure 3's error bars are on group means, not contrasts), and does not say whether the by-party breakdown was preregistered as primary. Since the paper's interpretive conclusion — that Republicans specifically drive the response to immigrant framing — rests on a three-way subgroup split with subgroup ns as small as 201, and since multiple outcome codings are examined (support-increase, support-decrease, maintain), the preregistration is doing important work that the article asks the reader to take on faith. It is available, which is why this is a verification instruction rather than a criticism; a reader who checks it will know exactly how much of the party-heterogeneity finding was planned.

Finally, the absence of any software or environment reporting is worth noting as a norm-compliance matter more than a practical obstacle. The models are OLS with two-way fixed effects and clustered standard errors — reproducible in any package — so no version dependency plausibly threatens the results. But combined with the missing archival replication package, it reflects a paper where the open-science machinery was applied thoroughly to the experiment and not extended to the observational analysis alongside it. Readers should calibrate accordingly: the survey findings are checkable today, the descriptive trends are checkable with an afternoon at nrs.ed.gov, and the regression findings require either author correspondence or a reconstruction whose fidelity you cannot confirm.
